technique: the turn — the exact line where picture becomes meaning, and how the poem earns it
poem:
Breath comes first, a slow and deepening draw,
the chest rising under the heaped quilt's heft,
and you lie a moment in your own warm weight
the way a stone lies settled in a field.
There's no hurry in you, none the day demands —
only the slow accounting of the body,
an ankle's small complaint, the shoulder's ease.
You turn, and the cool edge of the room comes in,
the smell of it like apples left too long,
a sweetness going brown and honest with it.
Then the floor, when your feet swing down to meet it —
boards you know by heart, their grain, their give.

The light's already warming the floor where you'll stand, patient as anything, just waiting for your feet.

So — up!
lesson: Today we learn one technique, the turn. The turn is the exact spot where a poem stops showing you a picture and starts meaning something, usually a shift in what the words are doing. This poem dilds a picture of waking up. It stays in the body, the slow accounting of the body, then an ankle's small complaint, the shoulders ease, then boards you know by heart. Those are facts about lying in bed. Then the poem turns on two words, so up. That line is not a picture, it is a command. Here is why it works on a listener. The poem keeps you still and slow for 12 lines, then it pushes you to stand. The sudden order feels earned because you already feel the weight it is asking you to leave. Try this, write six calm lines describing one moment, then end with a two-word command. The second time, listen for how all that slowness makes the last two words land hard. Here is the poem.
